newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian government approves 1997 draft budget.
newsitem.headline: Romanian government approves 1997 draft budget.

text.p: Romania's government has approved the draft of the 1997 state budget, a plank under loan accords with international lenders, Finance Minister Mircea Ciumara said on Saturday.

"This budget is a budget of responsibility. Everybody, including politicians, should understand the responsibility we have and that we must change the course of the country and steer it out of the current crisis," Ciumara told reporters.
Romania is confronted with high inflation, which hit 18.8 percent in February after prices of fuel, energy and food were liberalised, as well as with big state and trade deficits.
Under the 1997 bill, the consolidated budget deficit was forecast lower at 4.5 percent of the gross domestic product, against 5.8 percent in 1996.
Ciumara said he expected parliament to clear the draft within one month. The ruling centrist coalition has a comfortable majority in parliament.

The budget gap was agreed with the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank last month. Both institutions withheld loans for Romania over foreign exchange curbs and overspending by the former ruling leftists in the 1996 election year.
Romania hopes to get around $1.0 billion in total loans from the IMF and World Bank to underpin radical reforms.

Year-on-year inflation is seen at 89.5 percent against 56.9 in 1996. The government aims to cut monthly inflation to some 2.2 percent in the last months of 1997 after steps to slash deficits and push further privatisation and restructuring.
Romania also expects a 2.0 percent GDP fall in 1997 after a 4.1 percent growth last year.
The consolidated budget includes state budget, local government budgets, social security expenditure, supplementary pension funds and various other extra-budgetary funds.

The 1997 state budget revenues were envisaged at 40.4 trillion lei, with 41 percent coming from profit and wage taxation, while spendings were put at 52.81 trillion lei, of which 18 percent represent public debt expenditures.

"This year's state budget deficit was forecast at 5.4 percent of GDP," Ciumara said, adding that the bulk of the 1997 budget gap would be financed through external credits -- about 3.4 percent, with the rest funded by domestic loans.
Ciumara said funds for agriculture would amount to 2.3 percent of GDP. The defence budget, including education and health funds for the army, will take 2.85 percent of the GDP.
